7 Flows That Make or Break Your Customer Experience

When I started my manufacturing career, I spent most of my time optimizing machines and processes. Faster changeovers. Better OEE. Less breakdowns. Less Defects..

All important.

But over the years, I realized something uncomfortable: You can have excellent machines in a terrible system and the customer still feels the pain.

That's why 7 Flows of Manufacturing became one of my favorite lenses when I walk a shop floor: 

1️⃣ Raw materials flow – how smoothly do materials enter the plant, get stored, and reach the first value‑adding step without detours and double‑handling?

2️⃣ Components / sub‑assemblies flow – are parts always available at the right point-of-use, in the right quantity and sequence, or do operators wait and search?

3️⃣ WIP (work in process) flow – is product moving in small, leveled batches, or stuck in queues and pallets between processes?

4️⃣ Finished goods flow – do products leave the line and reach customers quickly, or sit in a “just in case” warehouse eating cash and space?

5️⃣ Operator (people) flow – can people perform their work safely with minimal walking, reaching, and motion, or is the layout forcing waste into every shift?

6️⃣ Engineering / equipment flow – how easily do changes, new designs, and machine improvements make their way into the process without chaos and firefighting?

7️⃣ Information flow – is the value stream driven by near real‑time data (clear signals, visual management, pull), or by emails, spreadsheets, and central scheduling pushing work everywhere?

During a Gemba walk now, I don’t just see conveyors, robots and forklifts. I ask a different question at each station:

🚨 “Where does this flow stop, pile up, or become unclear?”

Because every time flow stops, we silently create:
🔥 Longer lead times
🔥 More firefighting
🔥 Higher inventory and cost
🔥 Frustrated people and customers

The good news? Once you visualize it becomes much easier for teams to:
✅ Expose hidden queues and handovers
✅ Redesign layouts and logistics
✅ Align information signals with material movement
✅ Link daily management to real value streams

When you walk your factory tomorrow, try this simple exercise:
👉 Pick one product family.
👉 Follow it from dock to dock, 
👉 Ask: “Where does it stop, pile up, wait, or become unclear?”

Every interruption you find is an opportunity for safety, lead time, and cost improvement.

Curious: Which of these 7 flows is your biggest pain point today and how are you visualizing it with your teams?

Your Operators Aren’t the Problem, Their Workday Is : Non-Value Added Activities that Quietly Kills Efficiency

We spend millions on new machines, ERPs and automation… but quietly lose hours every single day in non‑value‑added activities on the shop floor from unnecessary motion and waiting to overprocessing, rework, set‑ups, inspections and information waste.

When you walk your factory with this lens, you start to see things differently:
🚫 Walking meters just to get a tool
🚫 Waiting for QA approval
🚫 Waiting for maintenance
🚫 Waiting for previous process
🚫 Standing idle for material
🚫 Trials, repeat adjustments 
🚫 Complex set‑ups eating time
🚫 100% checks to “inspect quality into” the product

Teams constantly searching:
🚫Drawings and work instructions
🚫Tools, Parts, Pallets
🚫Priorities and parameters
🚫 Someone to say “What’s next?”
🚫 Data written on paper, then retyped to Excel

None of these activities change the product in a way the customer is willing to pay for. But they do consume your most scarce resource: frontline time, energy and attention.

Turn the Sample Image Below into a simple Gemba tool:
✅ Print it in A3 and take it to the line.
✅ Ask operators: “Which of these icons do you see here?”
✅Let them point to:
     📌 Waiting
     📌Motion
     📌Transportation
     📌Overprocessing
     📌Defects & rework
     📌Inspections
     📌Set‑ups & adjustments
     📌Info & communication waste

Then run a quick “waste tally”:
🎯 Observe one operator for 30–60 minutes
🎯 Each time you see an activity that matches an icon, make a small mark
🎯 At the end you have a simple NVA profile of that job
🎯From there, start small Kaizens, not big projects:
🎯Pick one icon per area 

Co‑create a simple countermeasure with the team:
👉 Layout change
👉 5S action
👉 Visual standard
👉 Small poka‑yoke
👉 Celebrate quick wins to build momentum and trust

For new leaders and engineers, show that the biggest opportunities are often in how we use people’s time, not just in buying more equipment.

A mindset shift : The goal is not to blame operators.

In almost every case, the waste exists because of the SYSTEM: Layout, Standards, Planning, Information flow, Maintenance Practices, etc.

When we respect people’s time and make waste visible, we unlock huge potential in safety, quality, delivery and cost and make the workday less frustrating for our teams.

Obeya: The Visual Heart of Operational Excellence

Most factories try to manage performance in dozens of scattered meetings and slides. An Obeya Room does the opposite: it brings everything into one big visual room.

What is an Obeya ?  
An Obeya (“big room” in Japanese) is a dedicated physical or digital space where teams meet align on goals, priorities; track progress; prevent, fight with and solve problems. It is often called the “brain of Continous Improvement” because it concentrates goals, KPIs, problems, and actions in one visible place.

What does it do
✅ Aligns everyone on the same goals, priorities, and constraints
✅ Makes performance, risks, and bottlenecks visible at a glance
✅ Becomes the main place to review strategy, projects, customer voice, and daily operations

How does it work in practice?
🎯It is strategically situated at the heart of operations for easy access
🎯The walls (or screens) show KPIs, SQDCP, plans, Kaizens, risks, actions, and owners.
🎯Cross-functional teams stand up in short, rhythmic meetings (daily, weekly, monthly).
🎯Every routine follows a simple flow: review goals, review metrics, see gaps, escalate issues, assign actions, follow up
🎯Problems are surfaced visually and solved using structured methods instead of long email chains.

Key benefits of Obeya
🚩Faster, better decisions because all information and people are in one place.
🚩Stronger collaboration across functions, less silo thinking.
🚩Earlier detection of deviations and real-time course correction
🚩Higher accountability: everyone sees commitments, owners, and progress every day
🚩Clearer link from strategy (Hoshin) to daily execution and problem solving

In simple terms: an Obeya room turns your factory from “managing by scattered PowerPoints, Excels and email” into “managing by facts, visually, together, every day.” 

It is headquarters of a Visual CI Operating System

If your site already has Daily Management System, Boards and Asakai, the Obeya is the natural next step: One room where the whole story of your factory becomes visible.

Floor Markings : Simple Lines, Clear Rules, Organized Workspace, Higher Efficiency, Lower Incidents

Most people think Workplace Safety and 5S starts with procedures and ends with training. In reality, it often starts with a stripe of tape or a clear mark on the floor and a disciplined 5S culture behind it.

Your floor markings are silent supervisors:
✅ They tell you where to walk
✅ What to store where
✅ What to stay away from
✅ They reveal if something is missing
✅ They help newcomers to understand the area at one glance

If people don’t understand them, they become just “colorful decoration”. If everyone understands them, they become a daily safety and organization system.

Here’s a simple way to explain it on the shopfloor:
🟡 Yellow – Movement/Walkways
Aisles, walkways, traffic lanes. If you’re moving, you’re probably on yellow.
🟢 Green – Safe & OK
Finished goods and cleared items. Green means “ready to go”.
🔵 Blue – Beginning
Raw materials and incoming items. This is where the process starts.
🟠 Orange – Not yet
Hold and inspection. Something has to be checked before it continues.
🔴 Red – Stop
Scrap, defects, danger. If it’s red, you slow down your feet and speed up your brain. Stop touching anything in a red area without authorization.
⚫ Black – In progress
Work in progress – don’t mix it with finished goods.
⚪ White – Equipment
Parking spaces for trolleys, tools, racks, and equipment.
⚫⚪ Black–White – Access
Keep clear so people can reach what they need to operate or maintain.
⚫🟡 Black–Yellow – Hazard
Risk area. Only trained and authorized people belong here.
🔴⚪ Red–White – Emergency
Never ever to be blocked. This area is for emergency. Fire Protections, Exits, Other Safety Equipment  

You don’t need a 200‑page safety manual at every station. You need a floor that “talks” clearly enough that nobody can claim they didn’t see the risk or a potential issue.

🔄 Your move:
When was the last time you walked your lines instead of just your KPIs?
If you asked a new operator to explain your colors today, what would they say?

One quick conversation about floor markings this week might prevent one accident next week.

Safety Dashboard : Turning Safety Data Into Decisions That Save Lives

Previous two days I talked about Safety Risk Assessment and Safety Walks. Today, I want to introduce another important Visual Management tool : Safety Dashboard. 

Most companies talk about safety.  
Very few can see their risks before someone gets hurt.

What if you could see exactly:
🎯Where incidents and near misses happen,
🎯Which sites, shifts or contractors are most exposed,
🎯Which body parts are most often injured…  
and fix them before the next accident?

That’s what a Safety Dashboard does.  It is a single, visual platform that shows your critical safety metrics in real time and turns raw data into clear actions. 

It helps leaders monitor performance, spot patterns and prioritize the controls that actually reduce harm.

Key metrics I propose:
1️⃣ Total Recordable Incident Rate (TRIR) – all recordable injuries per 200,000 hours worked.  
2️⃣ Lost Time Injury Frequency Rate (LTIFR) – injuries with lost time per 1,000,000 hours worked.  
3️⃣ Near Miss Reporting Rate – how actively people are reporting hazards and close calls.  
4️⃣ Training Completion Rate – % of employees who completed mandatory safety training.  
5️⃣ Safety Compliance Rate – % of compliant items vs all applicable legal/standard items.  
6️⃣ First Aid Case Rate – first aid cases vs all injury cases.  
7️⃣ Mostly injured body parts – where to focus PPE and task redesign.  
8️⃣ Average time to close incidents/actions – how fast you respond and fix root causes.  
9️⃣ Safety perception scores – how safe employees feel, not just what the stats say.

Why Dashboard matters:
✅ Proactive risk management instead of reacting after accidents.
✅ Better compliance and easier audits.
✅ Sharper, data‑driven safety decisions.
✅ Stronger safety culture through visibility and accountability.

5S Is Not Housekeeping : It’s the Foundation How Your Whole Company Works

5S is a simple but powerful method to create a safe, organized and reliable workplace. It removes friction from daily work – people find what they need fast, problems become visible early, and standards are clear.

In many companies, 5S stops at production: lines are taped, tools are shadow‑boarded, floors are clean : while warehouses, offices and support areas stay chaotic. That local implementation creates islands of order in a sea of disorder.

5S Must Cover All Areas:
✅ Production is only one part of the value stream; poor 5S in other areas creates delays, quality issues, and safety risks
✅ Cross‑functional 5S makes information flow as good as material flow: tidy offices, clear documents, and organized planning reduces firefighting
✅ Companywide implementation sends a cultural message: “5S is how we work here,” not “something operators must do on the shop floor”

Every area touches the product or the information that drives the product: Production, assembly, maintenance, warehouse, offices. When all these zones apply the same 5 steps and the same discipline, materials flow, information flows and people can focus on real value instead of searching, waiting and correcting mistakes

5S Assessment is the mechanism to sustain
☑️ It verifies that standards are actually followed, not just written in a procedure.
☑️ It makes waste and abnormalities visible (clutter, unsafe operations, bad habits) before they turn into quality or safety problems
☑️ It creates data by scoring per area and per “S”. So you can compare functions, track trends and prioritize improvement actions
☑️ It reinforces ownership and discipline, because everyone knows what “good” looks like what NOT
☑️ It links 5S to results by showing how better organization improves productivity, safety, morale and quality over time

How to Perform the Assessment
🎯 Define scope and standards: List all areas to be audited 
🎯 Create a simple checksheet: For every question, add a numeric scale “actual vs. ideal” and GAP.
🎯 Standardize routine: Use the same checklist for all areas, assign auditors and frequency to follow progress

How to Visualize
👍 Use charts for each area to show the score of every S, so all dimensions visible at a glance.
👍 Add a simple gauge or bar showing the overall 5S score per area and for the whole company
👍 Use color‑coded dashboards or boards (green/yellow/red) where teams can see their latest scores, trends and key gaps

5S will never be “just cleaning” if it is measured, visualized and reviewed like any other key performance indicator : it becomes the backbone of safety, quality and delivery, and a daily signal of how seriously a company treats operational excellence.

Safety Walks : A Practical Guide - Embedding Safety in Daily Routine

Yesterday, I explained Safety Risk Assessment, today we'll go through another very important activity : Safety Walks - A systematic and disciplined approach to ensuring a safe working environment by observing, analyzing, and addressing potential risks.

🚨 What is a Safety Walk
A Safety Walk is a proactive measure where managers, supervisors, safety officers together with OPERATORS; tour the workplace to identify potential hazards and risks. It involves observing practices, interacting with employees, and promoting a safety culture.

How to Plan
1️⃣ Determine the Path : 
Determine checkpoints with a special Focus on high-risk areas or processes with recent incidents.
2️⃣ Select a Diverse Team: 
Include safety managers, supervisors, and frontline workers for diverse perspectives.
3️⃣ Develop a Checklist: 
Use detailed templates for PPE, equipment inspection, and facility conditions (example in illustration).

How to Conduct
👣 Briefing: 
Explain the purpose and review the checklist.
👣 Document Findings: 
Note hazards, non-compliance, and opportunities for improvement. Taking pictures and attaching them to report is highly recommended. A picture is worth thousand words.
👣 Interact with Employees: 
Gather insights on safety protocols and concerns.

Reporting and Actioning
1️⃣ Debriefing Session: 
Analyze findings, prioritize issues, and plan corrective actions.
2️⃣ Categorize and Prioritize: 
Use risk matrices to focus on high-severity hazards.
3️⃣ Daily Managament System : 
Make major findings first priority and agenda item in DMS/Asakai
4️⃣ Implement Corrective Actions: 
Assign tasks, set deadlines, and verify implementation.

Benefits
✅ Proactive Risk Management: 
Identify hazards before they become incidents.
✅ Behavioral Change: 
Address unsafe behaviors and reinforce safety protocols.
✅ Employee Engagement: 
Foster a culture where everyone contributes to safety.

Safety Walks are about fostering a culture of proactive engagement and accountability. By regularly conducting these walks, you empower every employee to take ownership of their safety, encourage open communication, and drive continuous improvement. 

The result? A safer, more resilient workplace where everyone thrives. 

And YES, Zero Accidents & Incidents are Possible !

Process Capability : A Practical One-Page Guide

What is Process Capability
Process capability is a statistical tool used to evaluate the ability of a process to produce output within specified limits, reflecting the "potential capability" of the process. It helps organizations determine if their processes can consistently meet customer requirements and specifications.

Purpose of Process Capability
🎯Meet customer requirements and specifications.
🎯 Measure and control the spread (variation) of the process.
🎯 Provide realistic tolerances for product dimensions.
🎯 Improve overall process performance capability.

Influencing Factors
➡️ Condition of machines and equipment.
➡️ Type and quality of raw materials.
➡️ Operator and inspector skill levels.
➡️ Measurement methods and instrument conditions.
➡️ Operational and environmental conditions.

Process Capability Overview
🔈 Voice of the Process: 
The actual output distribution of the process
🔈 Voice of the Customer: 
The specification limits set by the customer (USL and LSL)
🔈 Process Width vs. Design Width: 
The process should fit well within the design (specification) limits to be considered capable

Tools Used in Process Capability Analysis
1️⃣ Histogram: Shows the distribution of numerical data
2️⃣ Control Chart: Differentiates between common cause and special cause variation
3️⃣ Run Chart: Graphically represents how a process is performed or how data values change over time
4️⃣ ANOVA: Evaluates the difference between the means of more than two groups

Key Indices
↗️ Cp – Process Capability
Definition: Measures the ability of a process to produce output within specification limits, considering only the spread (variation) of the process
Interpretation: Cp does not account for how well the process is centered. A Cp ≥ 1.33 is generally considered acceptable

↗️ Cpk – Process Capability Index
Definition: Measures how close a process is running to its specification limits, accounting for process mean (centering)
Interpretation: Cpk considers both spread and centering. A Cpk ≥ 1.33 is desirable

Process capability analysis is essential for quality management, helping organizations ensure their processes are capable of consistently meeting customer requirements. By understanding and applying Cp and Cpk, businesses can identify improvement opportunities, reduce defects, and enhance customer satisfaction

From Hoshin to Gemba: Japanese KMI → KPI → KAI in Action

In many companies, performance management quickly becomes a jungle of disconnected numbers. Japanese management philosophy offers a very simple and powerful cascade that solves this: KMI → KPI → KAI

✅ KMI (Key Management Indicator): 
The “WHY”
KMIs are the few strategic indicators owned by top management. They describe what really matters for business over the term such as:
🎯 Safety, Health & Environment
🎯 Customer Engagement & Quality
🎯 People & Culture
🎯 Asset Utilization
🎯 Cost & Profitability

Think of KMIs as the North Stars on your dashboard : there should be only a few

✅ KPI (Key Performance Indicator):
The “WHAT”
KPIs translate each KMI into measurable process metric. One KMI is usually supported by several KPIs, but total set should still be lean (10 max for site). Examples :

Safety, Health & Environment: 
 -TRIR, Days Without Incident, Emissions
Asset Utilization: 
 - OEE, Throughput, Capacity Utilization
Customer Engagement & Quality: 
 - RFT, Claims, OTIF
Cost & Productivity : 
 - Unit Cost, Inventory Turnover, COPQ, Energy Consumption
People & Culture :
 - eNPS, Absenteeism, Turnover, Suggestions

✅ KAI (Key Activity Indicator):
The “HOW”
KAI's are specific actions at shop‑floor level that move the KPIs. They are concrete and small enough to be owned by a team. Examples :

To improve OEE; KAIs could be:
- Setup time ↓
- # of Breakdowns ↓
- MTBF ↑
- Short stops # ↓
To improve TRIR, KAIs could be:
- Observations # ↑
- Safety audits # ↑
- PPE compliance % ↑

2️⃣ Focused Improvement
Cross‑functional teams attack chronic losses with structured methods for hard, measurable gains

Prevent Before it Happens : Proactive Safety & Health Risk Assessment for Zero Accidents

Safety & Health Risk Assessment is a systematic process of identify workplace hazards, evaluate their risks, and implement control measures to minimize or eliminate potential harm. It ensures compliance with safety standards while fostering a culture of proactive risk management.

How to Perform*
1️⃣ Identify Hazards:
Walk through the workplace to identify potential hazards related to activities, equipment, materials, or processes.
2️⃣ Evaluate Risks:
Use a Risk Matrix to assess each hazard’s probability and impact. Assign a Risk Score based on likelihood (e.g., very likely to very unlikely) and severity (e.g., negligible to catastrophic). CATHASTROPHIC here is used for magnitute of the consequence is fatal.
3️⃣ Decide on Mitigation Actions:
For each hazard, define specific mitigation actions to reduce risk. For high-risk hazards (e.g., scores of 16-25), immediate actions like engineering controls or process redesign are recommended.
4️⃣ Assign Responsibilities and Deadlines:
Allocate tasks to responsible individuals and set deadlines for implementing mitigation measures. So close the loop.
5️⃣ Reassess Residual Risks:
After implementing mitigation actions, reassess the risk probability and impact to ensure the residual risk is either Low or Very Low, which could be acceptable until you mitigate all Cathastriphic, High and Medium risks.
6️⃣ Document Findings:
Keep detailed records of hazards, risk scores, mitigation actions, and outcomes for future reference.
7️⃣ Review and Update Regularly:
Periodically review the analysis to ensure it remains relevant as workplace conditions change.

Why to Perform
✅ Proactive Hazard Management: Identify and address risks before they cause harm.
✅ Improved Compliance: Ensure adherence to safety regulations and standards.
✅ Enhanced Decision-Making: Use data-driven insights to prioritize safety interventions.
✅ Continuous Improvement: Foster a culture of ongoing safety enhancement.
✅ Increased employee morale because of improved workplace safety standards

S&H Risk Assessment is not a compliance exercise, it’s the foundation of proactive safety culture.

Safety is a journey, not a destination - every step you take today builds a safer, more resilient workplace for tomorrow.

4 Competitive Zones: Where Operational Excellence Really Wins and Where It Wastes Time

Most companies still try to “be better at everything” – and then wonder why their Operational Excellence program feels busy but not strategic.

A more honest and useful lens is the 4 competitive zones – with a different OpEx playbook for each one.

1️⃣ Winning Zone – Where You Must Double Down
This is the sweet spot where:
- You are genuinely strong
- Customers truly care
- Competitors can’t easily match you
🎯 Here OpEx is about scaling and protecting your edge: World Class Manufacturing, standard work, rock‑solid OEE, a zero‑defect mindset and a relentless Kaizen engine. Every 1% improvement here compounds your competitive advantage.

2️⃣ Battleground Zone – Where Execution Decides the Winner
Everyone is playing here: you, your competitors and the customer.
- Use Value Stream Mapping to remove waste end‑to‑end
- Run focused Kaizen projects on the critical CTQs
- Shorten lead times, reduce breakdowns, tighten delivery reliability
🎯 Here OpEx focus shifts to speed, stability and cost. Whoever executes faster and more consistently wins the battleground.

3️⃣ Losing Zone – Where You Can’t Afford to Stay
The customer cares, but the competitor outperforms you.
Here you need ruthless clarity:
- Do we fix this (and how fast)?
- Do we partner or exit and focus elsewhere?
🎯 Here OpEx brings structure: gap analysis, structured problem solving, and focused improvement. The goal is not cosmetic change; it’s closing a survival‑critical gap or consciously walking away.

4️⃣ “Who Cares” Zone – Where Waste Likes to Hide
Both you and your competitors invest here, but the customer barely notices.
This is prime territory for:
- Complexity reduction
- “Stop‑doing” lists
- Reallocating resources into the Winning and Battleground zones
🎯 OpEx here is about freeing capacity, not polishing non‑value‑adding work.

When you look at your OpEx roadmap through these four lenses, priorities become painfully clear:
✅ Less “project shopping”
✅ More bets in the Winning Zone
✅ Faster decisions in the Losing Zone
✅ Fewer resources trapped in Who Cares

If you mapped your current initiatives onto these four zones today, how much of your OpEx effort is actually sitting in the wrong place?
